summary: Defines extensions to the Link Management Protocol so it can be used between a peer node and an adjacent optical line system. They are meant to meet the Optical Link Interface Requirements. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: The line equipment at each end of a long optical link knows how the link is set up and how it is doing. The routers at either end know what traffic is using it. This RFC lets a router ask the line equipment for the link's properties and for fault reports.

subtitle: How a router and the DWDM line equipment next to it exchange link properties and fault reports over LMP.

tldr.problem: The optical line systems at either end of a DWDM link know how the link is configured and what state it is in, but LMP only ran between peer nodes, so that knowledge never reached the routers at the ends.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends LMP so a peer node can hold a session with an adjacent optical line system, adding a CONFIG object that names the kind of session, six Data Link sub-objects that describe the link, and a group status object that reports faults.
tldr.outcome: Peer nodes learn the properties and the faults of the link from the equipment that owns it, which cuts manual configuration and improves fault detection. The extensions cover opaque line systems only, and RFC 4209 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 6898.

facts.label: Sub-object length
facts.value: At least 4 bytes, a multiple of 4

today: RFC 4209 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2005 that has since been updated by RFC 6898, and it has not been obsoleted. The text covers opaque optical line systems only, and leaves fully transparent wavelength routing for later work.

sections.title: Why the Line System Joins the Conversation
sections.content:
Networks are being developed with routers, switches, optical cross-connects (OXCs), dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) optical line systems (OLSes) and add-drop multiplexors (ADMs) that use a common control plane, such as Generalized MPLS (GMPLS), to provision resources dynamically and to provide network survivability with protection and restoration techniques.

The Link Management Protocol (LMP) is being developed as part of the GMPLS protocol suite to manage traffic engineering (TE) links. In its present form LMP focuses on peer nodes, meaning nodes that peer in signaling or routing, such as two OXCs. This document proposes extensions to LMP so it can be used between a peer node and an adjacent OLS, and the extensions are intended to satisfy the Optical Link Interface Requirements described in a companion document. The reader is assumed to be familiar with LMP as defined in the base specification.

Figure 1 of the RFC shows two peer nodes interconnected by a wavelength-multiplexed link, a DWDM optical link, with an OLS on each side of the span. Information about the configuration of this link and its current state is known by the two OLSes. Letting them communicate that information to the corresponding peer nodes over LMP can improve network usability by reducing the required manual configuration and by enhancing fault detection and recovery.

The information runs the other way too. The state of the label switched paths (LSPs) that use the link is known by the peer nodes, and passing it to the OLSes is useful for alarm management and link monitoring. Alarm management matters because the administrative state of an LSP, known to the peer nodes for example through the Admin Status object of GMPLS signaling, can be used to suppress spurious alarm reporting from the OLSes.

Figure 2 shows the extended model. A peer node may have LMP sessions with adjacent OLSes as well as with adjacent peer nodes. The peer-to-peer session between OXC1 and OXC2 is used to build the TE links used for GMPLS signaling and routing, while the OXC1-to-OLS1 and OXC2-to-OLS2 sessions are used to exchange information about the configuration of the DWDM optical link, its current state, and the state of the LSPs using that link. A peer node may have LMP sessions with one or more OLSes, and an OLS may have LMP sessions with one or more peer nodes.

A peer node maintains its peer-to-OLS sessions and its peer-to-peer sessions independently. It MUST therefore be possible for LMP sessions to come up in any order, in particular for a peer-to-peer session to come up in the absence of any peer-to-OLS sessions, and the other way round.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of device work together on a long optical link: routers at the ends, and the line equipment that carries the light between them. This RFC lets them exchange link information using the protocol the routers already use with each other.

sections.title: Scope: Opaque Line Systems
sections.content:
The RFC defines the vocabulary it uses. DWDM is dense wavelength division multiplexing and an OLS is an optical line system. A device is called X-opaque if it examines or modifies the X aspect of the signal while forwarding an incoming signal from input to output. A device is called X-transparent if it forwards incoming signals from input to output without examining or modifying that aspect of the signal. A Frame Relay switch is network-layer transparent, and an all-optical switch is electrically transparent.

This document focuses on the extensions required for use with opaque OLSes, and is intended for OLSes having SONET, SDH and Ethernet user ports.

At the time of writing, work was ongoing in the area of fully transparent wavelength routing. The RFC calls it premature to identify the information that would have to be exchanged between a peer node and an OLS in that context. The protocol described in the document nevertheless provides the framework in which additional information can be exchanged later if it is judged appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC covers line equipment that examines or changes the signal as it forwards it. Equipment that passes signals through untouched is left for later work, although the protocol leaves room to add it.

sections.title: Control Channel Management and the CONFIG Object
sections.content:
LMP consists of four main procedures, of which the first two are mandatory and the last two are optional: control channel management, link property correlation, link verification and fault management. All four functions are supported in LMP-WDM.

The RFC does not specify the exact implementation of the control channel. It could be, for example, a separate wavelength, a fiber, an Ethernet link, an IP tunnel routed over a separate management network, a multi-hop IP network, or the overhead bytes of a data link. Control channel management for a peer node-to-OLS link is the same as for a peer node-to-peer node link.

To tell a peer node-to-OLS session from a peer node-to-peer node session, the RFC defines a new LMP-WDM CONFIG object, with Class 6 and C-Type 2. The object carries two bits and a reserved field. The WDM bit indicates support for the LMP-WDM extensions defined in the document. The OLS bit says whether the sender is an optical line system, when it is set, or a peer node, when it is clear. The reserved field should be sent as zero and ignored on receipt.

The OLS bit allows a node to identify itself as an OLS or a peer node, which is used to detect the misconfiguration of a peer node-to-OLS session between two peer nodes, or of a peer node-to-peer node session between a peer node and an OLS. If a node does not support the LMP-WDM extensions, it MUST reply to the Config message with a ConfigNack message. If a peer node that is configured to run LMP-WDM receives a Config message with the OLS bit clear, it MUST also reply with a ConfigNack message.
sections.plainLanguage: When two devices open a session, each one says whether it is a router-like node or the line equipment. If the two sides are paired wrongly, the device that notices answers with a ConfigNack message.

sections.title: Link Verification Across the Span
sections.content:
The Test procedure used with OLSes is the same as in the base LMP specification. The VerifyTransportMechanism, included in the BeginVerify and BeginVerifyAck messages, allows nodes to negotiate a link verification method, and it is essential for line systems that have access to overhead bytes rather than to the payload. The VerifyId, provided by the remote node in the BeginVerifyAck message and used in all subsequent Test messages, differentiates Test messages from different link verification procedures. In addition to the Test procedure, the trace monitoring function of RFC 4207 may be used for link verification when the OLS user ports are SONET or SDH.

There is an interplay between the data links managed by peer-to-peer sessions and those managed by peer-to-OLS sessions. In the figure of the RFC, the OXC1-to-OLS1 session manages the data links between OXC1 and OLS1, and the OXC2-to-OLS2 session manages the data links between OXC2 and OLS2. The OXC1-to-OXC2 session, however, manages the data links between OXC1 and OXC2, which are actually a concatenation of the data links between OXC1 and OLS1, the DWDM span between OLS1 and OLS2, and the data links between OXC2 and OLS2. It is those concatenated links that comprise the TE links advertised in the GMPLS TE link state database.

The implication is that when the data links between OXC1 and OXC2 are being verified, OLS1 and OLS2 need to make themselves transparent with respect to these concatenated data links. Coordinating the verification of the OXC1-to-OLS1 and OXC2-to-OLS2 data links so that this transparency holds is the responsibility of the peer nodes, OXC1 and OXC2. It is also necessary for those peer nodes to understand the mappings between the data links of the peer node-to-OLS session and the concatenated data links of the peer node-to-peer node session.
sections.plainLanguage: To check the whole link, the line equipment on the way has to pass the test signal through without looking at it. The routers at the ends arrange that and keep track of which pieces belong to which path.

sections.title: Link Summarization and the New Sub-objects
sections.content:
The LinkSummary message is used to synchronize the Interface_Ids and to correlate the properties of the TE link. It includes one or more DATA_LINK objects, and the contents of a DATA_LINK object consist of a series of variable-length data items called Data Link sub-objects that describe the capabilities of the data links.

This document defines several additional Data Link sub-objects. The link characteristics they describe are, in general, those needed by the CSPF, the function that selects the path for a particular LSP. They describe the specified peer node-to-OLS data link as well as the associated DWDM span between the two OLSes.

Every sub-object starts with a Type field of 8 bits and a Length field of 8 bits. The Length field contains the total length of the sub-object in bytes, including the Type and Length fields, and it MUST be at least 4 and MUST be a multiple of 4. The reserved fields of the sub-objects below should be sent as zero and ignored on receipt.

  • Link Group ID, Type 3 and Length 8: a local ID assigned to a group of data links. Its main purpose is to reduce control traffic during failures that affect many data links, by allowing a single ChannelStatus message to cover a group of data links instead of one message for each data link. A data link may be a member of multiple groups, which is done by including multiple Link Group ID sub-objects in the LinkSummary message. The groups map the data links into the failable entities that the OLS knows about, so that if one of those entities fails, all the associated data links are failed and the peer node is notified with a single message. An OLS could create a Link Group for each laser, and one for each fiber, so that a loss of signal on a fiber is reported as one failure affecting all the data links on it. The Link Group ID 0xFFFFFFFF is reserved and indicates all data links in a TE link, and all data links are members of that group by default.
  • SRLG, Type 4 and Length (N+1)*4 where N is the number of SRLG values: identifies the shared risk link groups of which the data link is a member. This information may be configured on an OLS by the user and used for diverse path computation.
  • BER Estimate, Type 5 and Length 4: an estimate of the bit error rate of the data link. The bit error rate is the proportion of bits that have errors relative to the total number of bits received in a transmission, usually expressed as ten to a negative power. A rate of ten to the minus 13 means that out of every 10,000,000,000,000 bits transmitted, one bit may be in error. The 8-bit field holds the exponent, so a rate of ten to the minus X is sent as the value X. The rate is an indication of overall signal quality.
  • Optical Protection, Type 6 and Length 4: indicates whether the link is protected by the OLS. The information can be used as a measure of link capability, and it may be advertised by routing and used by signaling as a selection criterion. The encoding of the 6 link flags is defined in the GMPLS signaling specification.
  • Total Span Length, Type 7 and Length 8: the total distance of fiber in the OLS, held as a 32-bit unsigned integer that gives the total length of the WDM span in meters. It may be used as a routing metric or to estimate delay.
  • Administrative Group, also called Color, Type 8 and Length 8: the administrative group to which the data link belongs, held as a 32-bit value.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new sub-object is a small record about one link: which failure group it belongs to, how clean the signal is, whether a backup path exists, and how long the fiber is. The routing function reads these records when it chooses a path.

sections.title: Fault Management and Group Status
sections.content:
The fault management procedure used between a peer and an OLS follows the procedures of the base LMP specification, with some further extensions defined here. The information learned from the OLS-to-peer fault management procedures may be used to trigger peer-to-peer LMP fault management, or may be used to trigger GMPLS signaling and routing procedures directly.

Fault management consists of three major functions: fault detection, fault localization and fault notification. The fault detection mechanisms are the responsibility of the individual nodes and are not specified as part of this protocol. They may include a bit error rate exceeding a threshold, and loss of signal and SONET or SDH level errors. It is the responsibility of the OLS to translate these failures into (Signal) OK, Signal Failure or Signal Degrade.

The OLS uses the messages defined in the LMP fault localization procedures, ChannelStatus, ChannelStatusAck, ChannelStatusRequest and ChannelStatusResponse, to inform the adjacent peer node of failures it has detected, in order to initiate the LMP fault localization procedures between the peer nodes. It does not participate in those procedures itself. The OLS may also run its own fault localization process, so that it can determine the location of a fault along the DWDM span, for example pinpointing the fault to a particular amplifier in a span of thousands of kilometers in length.

Each data link is identified by an Interface_ID, and a Link Group ID may also be assigned to a group of data links. To report the status of a group instead of each link, the RFC defines a new LINK_GROUP CHANNEL_STATUS object, with Class 13 and C-Type 4. It carries a 32-bit Link Group ID, two flag bits shown as A and D in the RFC's diagram, and a 32-bit Channel Status value whose values are defined in the base LMP specification. The object may be used in place of the CHANNEL_STATUS objects in a ChannelStatus message, and it is non-negotiable.
sections.plainLanguage: When a laser or a fiber fails, the line equipment sends one message that covers every link affected. The router at the end then starts the fault location procedure, while the line equipment may look for the fault itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: LMP message security uses IPsec, as described in the base LMP specification. This document only defines new LMP objects that are carried in existing LMP messages, so it introduces no other new security considerations beyond those already covered in the base specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages are protected in the same way as in the base protocol, so there is nothing new to guard here.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
LMP defines four name spaces and the ways in which IANA can make assignments to them: the LMP Message Type, the LMP Object Class, the LMP Object Class type (C-Type), which is unique within the Object Class, and the LMP Sub-object Class type (Type), which is unique within the Object Class.

This memo introduces the following new assignments. Under the CONFIG class name it allocates LMP-WDM_CONFIG with C-Type 2. Under the CHANNEL_STATUS class name it allocates LINK_GROUP with C-Type 4. Under the DATA_LINK class name it allocates the sub-object types Link_GroupId (3), SRLG (4), BER_Estimate (5), Optical_Protection (6), Total_Span_Length (7) and Administrative_Group (8).
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives every new object and field a number so that two devices agree on which is which. The numbers are listed in the section itself.

fields.name: WDM

fields.desc: Set when the sender is an optical line system, clear when the sender is a peer node.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Should be sent as zero and ignored on receipt.

fields.desc: Total length of the sub-object in bytes, including Type and Length.

fields.desc: Should be sent as zero and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Link Group ID
fields.desc: Local ID of a group of data links. The value 0xFFFFFFFF means all data links in a TE link.

items.label: Link_GroupId
items.desc: Group of data links that fail together, such as one laser or one fiber.

items.label: SRLG
items.desc: The shared risk link groups the data link belongs to.

items.label: BER_Estimate
items.desc: The exponent of the bit error rate, so a rate of ten to the minus X is sent as X.

items.label: Optical_Protection
items.desc: Whether the optical line system protects the link.

items.label: Total_Span_Length
items.desc: Total length of the WDM span in meters, as a 32-bit unsigned integer.

items.label: Administrative_Group
items.desc: The administrative group, or color, the data link belongs to.
